text:
final thoughts on this book, the art of memoir, and autobio

1/3. these are extremely hard to write well...about as high-risk/high-reward as u can get. 

the truth is that there is no way to write effectively about one's life, without speaking about life as it really was -- and that includes whatever took place involving the people around you.

in a good memoir or autobio, u know early on: "mfs must be HEATED that he wrote this."

this is unavoidable

and u can tell equally quickly, in the other direction, when a book has been whitewashed or when a man's life story doesn't ring true to, well, real life

the approach, which Agassi gets right, is "I’m going to hold myself accountable first and foremost."

Others are a distant second to that, but if you are brutally honest and harsh on your own conduct, and show true courage in tearing yourself down, it becomes much harder for ppl to push back when they get a lesser version of that same treatment.

because the truth is the truth. what happened, happened, and if you don't like what you said or did, perhaps you shouldn't have said or done it in the first place?

there is an enormous amount of tact involved here in knowing what to include vs exclude, and you don't want to bring other people's past into it unless absolutely necessary...but there is no way to recount a life, that doesn't include others.

and Agassi is just as complementary of some players (Federer) as he is negative of others (Chang, Becker, sometimes Sampras).

overall, Agassi/Moehringer nailed the balance here

2/3. this is a true self-help book

"self-help" is a horseshit category, most of what u see that is new or on twtr, is recycling other people's wisdom, or trying to share the lessons of another man's hardship story

the issue is that it rings hollow immediately

if the hardest thing you've ever been through is "I was disillusioned by my finance job," the writing is going to be awful...u can def sell a few copies but the book will be forgotten in less than a year

true heroism, true self-help, is to pull a mirror out and show the world the ugliest sides of yourself

the reader will examine their own flaws accordingly, in private, and this is how you get another man to change.

3/3. no explaining, no neat packaging

the last thing this book does exceptionally well, is it doesn't feel the need to explain, to rationalize one's behavior, or conclude everything with a neat lesson about life

life is messy

a book about life should be messy, it should just vomit pain and suffering, bleeding out for the reader and saying "here"

if its too neat its fugazi

if you've read any of Trump's books, this is the flaw they all suffer from...there's bits of wisdom, but he's mostly trying to paint a picture of himself. he wants to portray an image and the writing suffers as a result

same issue with Rousseau's "Confessions" and many other autobios

the way you write a really good one of these books, is to tell how you felt AT THAT TIME.  not how you feel today, about what happened back then.

this is extraordinarily difficult and means unpacking and unwiring your brain, wading through the primordial soup of memory

and the lessons here are presented in a way that isn't mawkish or overly sentimental...very hard to understand what he means here, unless you've been there, in which case you recognize it as 100% truth:

“I know for sure that there's pain in life. We have to fight through our pain and find a way to get through it. Life is about fighting through that pain and, when you can, easing the pain of others.”

END

the positive of reading this Agassi book in 2026, rather than when it was published in 2009, is that we've had a chance to see if anything came out as bogus

nada...some ppl were pissed, but nada.

any criticism u can find, it mostly falls flat.

that's how u know its a winner

great read and esp if you're a writer, or intend to write truthfully about your own life, I would take very very careful notes on how this was done...I cannot think of others who have executed better on the category than Agassi and Moehringer.

quotedTweet.text:
incredible book from 2009...kept seeing this on "best autobios ever" lists, almost looked out of place, but it isnt.

much credit due to co-author J.R. Moehringer who is just a dazzingly good writer, a master hand, one of the best I can remember coming across

the two of them, plus the entire team that helped put this together, transcended the genre...really isn't a sports book or tennis book at all, it covers the following topics as well as anything I've ever read:

-self-mastery/knowledge of self...the three enemies, the game + the opponent + the self: this applies for pretty much any endeavor but you have the game (in this case, say, swinging a racket). 

then you have the opponent who you are playing, sometimes even moreso than the game -- boxing, poker come to mind. 

finally, you have you against YOURSELF. you can know the game and know your opponent ice cold...but if u aren't master of self, and if u cant execute, all that other shit doesnt matter...u are ur own worst enemy.

I think of this a lot bc people see all these book recs (whether markets or otherwise), esp if younger, and are like "what order should I tackle these"

by laying it out as 3 enemies...it makes a little more sense

-"swinging the racket," the game, has to be #1, those are the fundamentals. master those first
-"know thy opponent" is second...this is more, understanding human nature and psychological/emotional biases
-"know thyself" is third and final, the hardest and the lifelong one

u cant qualify for the US Open if u cant swing the racket

then, u have all players studying one another's weaknesses

but when it comes down to the final...like agassi/sampras, its gonna come down to who is "master of self"

amazing quote in there: "the fifth set has nothing to do with tennis."

entirely about breaking your opponent's will, conditioning...stuff u see in all sports, momentum, like where your opponent throws their absolute best stuff, and u take it and ur still standing

thats when u see the look in their face, thats when u know they are broken

and thats when u smoke their fucking boots.

-success/failure 2x...internal/external...how hollow victory is, how all pain is 2x any victory: King Solomon-esque, and a ton of credit is due to Moehringer here

these are extremely complex topics to handle well and he shapes Agassi's story into these sort of eternal frameworks

the notion that, the entire world can view you as a success, ranked #1 in the world, but you look in the mirror and all you see is failure...you feel nothing

and then at the bottom when the world sees u as a failure but u dont feel that way at all

almost 0 correlation between this 4-way "mirror" for lack of a better word (success/failure/internal/external), a theme u see over and over in amazing stories like these...the way u feel abt urself is laughably disconnected from the way the world feels about you

and then the pain of failure far exceeding the thrill of victory...something u see over and over as well

losing in the finals of a slam, hurts 2x as bad as winning a slam feels

but you see this in so many other books that its not tennis specific, thats what I mean by how the book transcends the genre...tons in here directly applicable to markets, same way if u were to ask "what was jiro dreams of sushi" about, u know sushi is the absolute last thing.

more later, I rarely take notes while reading but this one had me going...tons of screenshots of quotes/excerpts....I don't think any book is a 10/10, but for the autobio genre, this is as close to a 10/10 as u will find.
